catalog_quote: Stress still needs to be investigated in greater detail. However, some preliminary findings shall be outlined here. Stress is free in the sense that its position cannot be predicted for any word from general phonological rules. Stress seems to be lexically conditioned. It may fall on the first syllable of bisyllabic words: bisyllabic word, 1st syllable stressed: "rE.ŋE ’woman’ "maŋ.ra ’money’ ... "la.ka ’v. dance’ "kpa.ra ’flying fox’ Note that in most of these examples, the first and the second syllable both lack a coda and are thus ’light’ syllables. In bisyllabic words, stress may also be on the second syllable, and this seems to be the case where at least the second syllable is closed and thus ’heavy’: bisyllabic word, 2nd syllable stressed: lak."lak ’v. dance (red)’ va."Pal ’banana’ Paŋ."sar ’person’ ... With trisyllabic words, stress is on the last syllable: ... trisyllabic word, last syllable stressed: Paŋ.sa."ra ’person’ na.na."ra ’tree sp.’ lak.la."ka ’n. dance’ ... In the following examples, stress is on the penultimate syllable of what appears to constitute a trisyllabic word: mi."mi.jefi ’red’ sefi.sefi.jE ’different’ vu."nuofi ’island, village’ ... However, this stress pattern in these examples may resemble evidence for the existence of heavy nuclei in Vera’a consistiing of a vowel clusters, so that consequently we are dealing with bisyllabic words in these instances. ... As noted above, stress in Vera’a still needs to be investigated in greater detail.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the seventeen Torres-Banks languages as a group (Vera'a among them), François states that after the loss of word-final unstressed vowels, stress now falls on the final syllable (historically the penult). He does not state a Vera'a-specific rule; his own Vera'a data (p. 464, Table 4 p. 476) show that Vera'a alone among the Vanua Lava languages retains a word-final echo vowel (Vf) that is unstressed and elidable phrase-medially, so a uniform 'final stress' reading cannot be projected onto Vera'a words that end in an echo vowel (stress would sit on the last full vowel, i.e. the penult of such words). An unpublished claim on Wikipedia (editor edit summary 2023-10-04: 'Vera'a and Mota have lost penult stress.. These are now stress-less lgs'; article sentence added 2023-11-11: 'There is no stress in Veraʼa') contradicts the area-level final-stress statement. The primary description (Schnell 2011/2010) could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only historical: protoforms 'received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward' (p. 451); nothing synchronic for Vera'a.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedge 'essentially all the languages of the area'. Vera'a-specific caveat p. 464: 'This suggests that the final vowel Vf of Vera'a has a specific elidable status when (and only when) it proceeds from a posttonic [+low] V2 in a process of vowel reduction' (VRA 'ala 'clam' final /a/ contrasted with the 'final stressed' schwa of Lo-Toga); Table 4 p. 476 VRA: '[-sonorous] > Ø / [+sonorous] > Vf'. Wikipedia (uncited, editor-origin) says there is no stress in Vera'a at all. Note the text of the PDF renders the 'fi' ligature as '²'; 'final' restored in the quote.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, comparative-historical claim about citation forms; phrase-level effect noted: the Vera'a echo vowel is dropped phrase-medially (naka 'canoe' > nak susu, p. 464). No instrumental or synchronic prosodic description of Vera'a was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Vera'a [vra] was split off from 'Vatrata' [vlr] together with Lemerig [lrz] by ISO change request 2008-069; our earlier rosters carried it under the retired code vatr1237. François abbreviates it VRA. The Wikipedia editor's claim ('Vera'a and Mota have lost penult stress') also concerns Mota (mota1237). No dialect issue: the language is spoken in the single village of Vera'a on Vanua Lava.

new_statements.relation_note: This held text IS the source of the catalog's 'lexical' record (same section, same wording); nothing new beyond confirming the full sec. 2.3 incl. the heavy-syllable and trisyllable-final tendencies already summarised; It stands against the unsourced Wikipedia line 'There is no stress in Vera'a' and is more specific than François 2005's area-level 'final stress' claim (both already held by the project).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Author's own classification: stress is free / lexically conditioned and not predictable by general rule (preliminary). Observed tendencies: light-light disyllables stressed on the first syllable (ˈrɛŋɛ 'woman', ˈmaŋra 'money', ˈlaka 'dance', ˈkpara 'flying fox'); disyllables with a closed (heavy) second syllable stressed on the second (lakˈlak, vaˈʔal 'banana', ʔaŋˈsar 'person', mamˈgin 'cold'); trisyllables stressed on the last syllable (ʔaŋsaˈra, nanaˈra, laklaˈka).
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent penultimate stress in some seeming trisyllables (miˈmijɛ 'red', vuˈnuo 'island, village', duˈruo '3dl') is reanalysed as disyllables with a heavy vowel-cluster nucleus (glide epenthetic); author twice flags the analysis as preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Schnell 2011 describes Vera'a (Vatrata, ISO vra) as spoken in Vera'a village on the west coast of Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, North Vanuatu, from his DoBeS fieldwork corpus (2007 onward); the grammar is the reworked sketch grammar of his 2010 Kiel PhD thesis. ELAR dk0681 documents Uruangnirin (Karas Islands, West Papua, Indonesia), unrelated.

readall_conflicts: No new conflict. The only descriptive source, Schnell 2011 sec. 2.3 (held full text), calls Vera'a stress free/lexically conditioned with weight- and length-linked tendencies (light-light disyllables initial, closed final syllable stressed, trisyllables final) and flags the analysis as preliminary; the catalog's 'lexical' record is taken from exactly this passage, so the copy consulted agrees with the catalog. Already held by the project and unchanged: François 2005 p. 451 asserts final stress area-wide for the Banks/Torres languages without Vera'a-specific placement data, and the English Wikipedia sentence 'There is no stress in Vera'a' is unsourced (traced to a 2023 edit summary). Work 0 (ELAR dk0681) is not a Vera'a source at all: the deposit is Eline Visser's Uruangnirin documentation, mis-attached to Vera'a via a page-foot footnote in the Multi-CAST overview.
